name: Juan Santamaría International Airport
before:
Costa Rica's main airport and second busiest in Central America after Panama, 20 km north west of downtown San José in Alajuela Province. It handled 5 million passengers in 2022.

Terminals are simple but worth checking. International flights use the Main Terminal and domestic flights the Domestic Terminal, so a client connecting from a long haul arrival onto a Sansa flight has to change buildings.

The route map is broader than Liberia's, the country's other international airport. Both reach North and Central America and Europe, but San José also serves South America and the Caribbean. Avianca is the largest international operator, followed by Copa. jetBlue and United run the most year round United States destinations, and Iberia is the only European airline flying daily all year.

The single runway takes wide bodies, with A330s, A350s, 777s and 787s all operating scheduled services. A Concorde landed here for an airshow in 1999.

It is named after Juan Santamaría, the drummer boy who died in 1856 defending Costa Rica against William Walker's forces.
after:
Costa Rica's main airport, in Alajuela, 20 km north west of downtown San José. It handled more than 6.5 million passengers in 2025.

Sansa, the largest domestic airline, recommends allowing at least five hours to connect from an international flight to one of its own.

The route map is broader than that of Liberia, the country's other main international airport. Both reach North America and Europe, but San José also serves South America and the Caribbean. The civil aviation authority's 2024 figures put Copa, American, United and Avianca among the largest international airlines here. European airlines include British Airways, Iberia, Air France, KLM, Lufthansa and Edelweiss. British Airways flies from London Gatwick, and says the service moves to Heathrow from 25 October 2026, five times a week.

The single runway takes wide-bodied jets.

It is named after Juan Santamaría, Costa Rica's national hero.

claims.claim: Costa Rica's main airport
claims.note: The Tourism Board's live page calls it the country's main airport; Panrotas, reporting Motiva's 2025 results, calls it the largest in Costa Rica; DGAC's 2024 yearbook gives it 6,508,042 passengers against 1,921,345 at Daniel Oduber Quirós (Liberia) and fewer than 30,000 at each of the other two international airports. The operator's own site (sjoairport.com, which OurAirports and Wikipedia both give) answered the link lister with a Cloudflare block page (HTTP 403), so it was left alone and nothing here rests on it.

claims.claim: more than 6.5 million passengers in 2025
claims.inAfter: It handled more than 6.5 million passengers in 2025.
claims.note: Was '5 million passengers in 2022'. A passenger total replaces a passenger total. Motiva, which owned the concession holder Aeris until 1 September 2026, reports 6,554 thousand total passengers for Aeris in 2025, up 3.2 per cent on 6,349 thousand; Panrotas reports the same 3.2 per cent growth for Juan Santamaría, and DGAC's yearbook names Aeris as the source of its Juan Santamaría figures, which ties the Aeris row to this airport. Wikipedia's infobox gives 6,707,096 for 2025 (footnoted to the Costa Rican AIP and DGAC). The two differ by about 2 per cent (DGAC's 2024 total of 6,508,042 is likewise above Motiva's 6,349 thousand, so the two counts are defined differently); both are above 6.5 million, hence 'more than 6.5 million'.

claims.claim: named after Juan Santamaría, Costa Rica's national hero
claims.inAfter: It is named after Juan Santamaría, Costa Rica's national hero.
claims.note: Was 'named after Juan Santamaría, the drummer boy who died in 1856 defending Costa Rica against William Walker's forces'. The Juan Santamaría Historical and Cultural Museum in Alajuela (a state museum, .go.cr) names him the national hero and is devoted to the national campaign of 1856 to 1857 against the filibuster invasion; its own biography of him is a scanned PDF with no readable text, so the drummer boy, the year of his death and William Walker rest on Wikipedia alone (cut below).
